conflicts.point: Whether centralized physical infrastructure controls on large-scale compute clusters constitute an effective and enforceable chokepoint against unauthorized model proliferation.

positions.stance: Large-scale compute clusters require visible electrical and hardware supply chains, providing an inspectable regulatory chokepoint that prevents unverified frontier model development.
Hardware gating fails to contain proliferation because sub-threshold training runs and decentralized clusters account for substantial frontier-adjacent experimentation beyond regulatory reach.

conflicts.point: Whether pre-market safety reviews for dual-use artificial intelligence models are necessary to prevent irreversible harms or function primarily as anticompetitive protectionism.

positions.stance: Preventing catastrophic biological or cyber misuse through mandatory pre-market certification outweighs the costs of market consolidation and delayed open-source release.
The societal benefits of open-source diffusion and decentralized innovation outweigh speculative catastrophic risks, rendering pre-market gates an unacceptable barrier to progress.

verdicts.conflict: Whether centralized physical infrastructure controls on large-scale compute clusters constitute an effective and enforceable chokepoint against unauthorized model proliferation.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic position cites specific empirical data showing that sub-threshold training runs utilizing fewer than four thousand accelerators account for thirty percent of frontier-adjacent experimentation. This concrete metric demonstrates that hardware gating misses a substantial segment of development activity, whereas the safetyist position relies on abstract assertions about electrical supply chains without addressing sub-threshold leakage.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence proving that sub-threshold training runs cannot achieve frontier capabilities or that secondary clusters can be comprehensively tracked via power consumption audits would restore the viability of centralized controls.

verdicts.conflict: Whether pre-market safety reviews for dual-use artificial intelligence models are necessary to prevent irreversible harms or function primarily as anticompetitive protectionism.
verdicts.rationale: Both positions highlight valid systemic concerns without capturing the entire problem space. The safetyist camp correctly identifies the irreversible nature of public weight distribution, while the accelerationist and skeptic camps correctly identify the market consolidation risks of high regulatory compliance costs. Neither side provides a mechanism to reconcile irreducible safety harms with open ecosystem benefits.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical validation of verifiable technical mechanisms that allow safe public weight releases without enabling catastrophic misuse would resolve this tension.
